"'''Honey'''", also known as "'''Honey (I Miss You)'''", is a song written by [[Bobby Russell]]. He originally produced it with former [[Kingston Trio]] member [[Bob Shane]], who was the first to release the song. It was then given to American singer [[Bobby Goldsboro]], who recorded it for his 1968 [[Honey (Bobby Goldsboro album)|album of the same name]], originally titled ''Pledge of Love''. Goldsboro's version was a hit, reaching No. 1 in several countries.<ref name="countrydaily">{{cite web
 | title= Back in 1968, this was a No.1 Hit, "Honey" by Bobby Goldsboro
 | first= Grant | last= King
 | date=  February 2, 2018
 | work=  countrythangdaily.com
 | url =  https://www.countrythangdaily.com/honey-bobby-goldsboro/}}</ref>

In the song, the narrator mourns his absent wife, and the song begins with him looking at a tree in their garden, remembering how "it was just a twig" on the day she planted it. Only in the third verse is it finally revealed that "one day...the angels came," and that his wife had died.
The chorus was used in Evangeline by [[Stephen Sanchez]].

"Honey", also known as "Honey (I Miss You)", is a song written by Bobby Russell. He originally produced it with former Kingston Trio member Bob Shane, who was the first to release the song. It was then given to American singer Bobby Goldsboro, who recorded it for his 1968 album of the same name, originally titled Pledge of Love. Goldsboro's version was a hit, reaching No. 1 in several countries.

In the song, the narrator mourns his absent wife, and the song begins with him looking at a tree in their garden, remembering how "it was just a twig" on the day she planted it. Only in the third verse is it finally revealed that "one day...the angels came," and that his wife had died.
The chorus was used in Evangeline by Stephen Sanchez.

sections.heading: Composition and recordings
sections.wikitext:
"Honey" was written by [[Bobby Russell]], who took inspiration from a tree in his front yard when he noticed how big it had become since he had planted it. From this came the first line of the song, "See the tree, how big it's grown ...".<ref name="bronson">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RVFLAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA239 |title=The Billboard Book of Number One Hits |first= Fred |last=Bronson |date= 1997|isbn=9780823076413 |publisher=Billboard Books|page=239}}</ref>  His song was first recorded by [[Bob Shane]] of [[The Kingston Trio]], produced by Russell himself.<ref name="bronson"/> 

Before Shane's recording was released, Goldsboro was recommended the song by [[Larry Henley]] of [[the Newbeats]]. However, Goldsboro thought the recording by Shane was over-produced and the lyrics overpowered by the production.<ref name="bronson"/><ref name="hyatt">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8ZxHAAAAMAAJ |title=The Billboard Book of Adult Contemporary Hits |first=Wesley |last=Hyatt |date= 1999|isbn=9780823076932 |publisher=Billboard Books|page=239}}</ref> Goldsboro at that time was in need of songs to record, he and his producer Bob Montgomery invited Russell over to play a few of his songs, which included "Honey". After listening to Russell's simpler rendition accompanied by just a guitar, Goldsboro became interested and asked if he could cover the song.<ref name="hyatt"/> Russell was initially reluctant as Shane's version was due to be released, but eventually agreed that Goldsboro could record it as long as his single did not compete with Shane's record. They agreed to delay the release of Goldsboro's recording by four weeks.<ref name=bickhart /><ref name=reynolds /> 

The song was recorded on January 30, 1968,<ref name=reynolds>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0lV-DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA34 |title=The Music of Bobby Goldsboro |first= Robert|last= Reynolds |date=2018 |page=34 |publisher=Lulu.com |isbn=9780359235711 }}</ref> with an arrangement by Don Tweedy. Goldsboro later attributed the success of the song to Tweedy's arrangement, and believed that Shane could have the same success with Tweedy's arrangement.<ref name="hyatt"/> According to Goldsboro, the recording session for the song went so well, the first take was completely satisfactory; it was decided to record another take just to see if it could be improved upon and it came out just as well, so the first take was released as the single.<ref name=bickhart>{{cite magazine|title=Watching Bobby Grows: A Decade of Hits |first=Jim |last=Bickhart |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tgcEAAAAMBAJ&pg=RA1-PA1962 |magazine=Billboard |date= October 5, 1974 |pages=BG-3, 4, 8}}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media |url= https://open.spotify.com/track/5JBFh2mjUWvSarLCbXyG1f|title=Bobby Goldsboro Interview (2011), Stuart Cameron |via=Spotify|time=13:05–14:20}}</ref>
sections.text:
"Honey" was written by Bobby Russell, who took inspiration from a tree in his front yard when he noticed how big it had become since he had planted it. From this came the first line of the song, "See the tree, how big it's grown ...".  His song was first recorded by Bob Shane of The Kingston Trio, produced by Russell himself. 

Before Shane's recording was released, Goldsboro was recommended the song by Larry Henley of the Newbeats. However, Goldsboro thought the recording by Shane was over-produced and the lyrics overpowered by the production. Goldsboro at that time was in need of songs to record, he and his producer Bob Montgomery invited Russell over to play a few of his songs, which included "Honey". After listening to Russell's simpler rendition accompanied by just a guitar, Goldsboro became interested and asked if he could cover the song. Russell was initially reluctant as Shane's version was due to be released, but eventually agreed that Goldsboro could record it as long as his single did not compete with Shane's record. They agreed to delay the release of Goldsboro's recording by four weeks. 

The song was recorded on January 30, 1968, with an arrangement by Don Tweedy. Goldsboro later attributed the success of the song to Tweedy's arrangement, and believed that Shane could have the same success with Tweedy's arrangement. According to Goldsboro, the recording session for the song went so well, the first take was completely satisfactory; it was decided to record another take just to see if it could be improved upon and it came out just as well, so the first take was released as the single.

sections.heading: Release
sections.wikitext:
Goldsboro's recording of "Honey" was released as a [[single (music)|single]] in the U.S. in February 1968. While Shane's recording reached only 104 on the Bubbling Under chart,<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rQoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA71-IA7 |magazine=Billboard|title=Bubbling Under The Hot 100|date=April 13, 1968 }}</ref> Goldsboro's version became successful very quickly, and reached the top of the chart in April. It spent five weeks at No. 1 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] singles chart (the 200th song to reach No. 1 on that chart), from April 7 to May 11, and three weeks atop ''Billboard''{{'s}} [[Hot Country Songs|Hot Country Singles]] chart. It was preceded on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 by "[[(Sittin' on) the Dock of the Bay]]" by [[Otis Redding]] and was followed by [[Archie Bell & the Drells]]' "[[Tighten Up (Archie Bell & the Drells song)|Tighten Up]]". It was Goldsboro's only No. 1 hit on the Pop Singles and Country Singles charts and it was his first song to top the [[Hot Adult Contemporary Tracks|Adult Contemporary chart]]. ''Billboard'' ranked the record as the No. 3 song for 1968.<ref>[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1968]]</ref>

"Honey" reached No. 2 on the [[UK Singles Chart]] on its initial release in 1968, and a re-release of the single in the [[United Kingdom]] in 1975 also reached No. 2.<ref name=ukchart /> In Australia, it spent four weeks at No. 1 on the [[ARIA Charts]], replacing [[the Beatles]]' "[[Lady Madonna]]", and was the No. 6 song of 1968.{{cn|date=September 2022}}
sections.text:
Goldsboro's recording of "Honey" was released as a single in the U.S. in February 1968. While Shane's recording reached only 104 on the Bubbling Under chart, Goldsboro's version became successful very quickly, and reached the top of the chart in April. It spent five weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 singles chart (the 200th song to reach No. 1 on that chart), from April 7 to May 11, and three weeks atop Billboard{{'s}} Hot Country Singles chart. It was preceded on the Billboard Hot 100 by "(Sittin' on) the Dock of the Bay" by Otis Redding and was followed by Archie Bell & the Drells' "Tighten Up". It was Goldsboro's only No. 1 hit on the Pop Singles and Country Singles charts and it was his first song to top the Adult Contemporary chart. Billboard ranked the record as the No. 3 song for 1968.

"Honey" reached No. 2 on the UK Singles Chart on its initial release in 1968, and a re-release of the single in the United Kingdom in 1975 also reached No. 2. In Australia, it spent four weeks at No. 1 on the ARIA Charts, replacing the Beatles' "Lady Madonna", and was the No. 6 song of 1968.{{cn|date=September 2022}}

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext:
"Honey" was immediately and immensely popular. It sold a million copies in its first three weeks,<ref name="Billboard74"/>{{rp|BG4}} the fastest-selling record in the history of United Artists.<ref name="billboard-apr-13">{{cite periodical
 | url=  https://books.google.com/books?id=rQoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA8
 | title='Honey' Honey Single for UA
 | magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]
 | date= April 13, 1968
 | quote=Bobby Goldsboro's 'Honey' is the fastest selling single in United Artist's 10-year history... The disk has been certified by the RIAA as a million seller after only four weeks on the market.
}}</ref><ref name=goldsboro>{{cite web
 | url=  https://www.bobbygoldsboro.com/home.cfm
 | title=Bobby Goldsboro - The Website of Bobby Goldsboro!
 | work= bobbygoldsboro.com
}}</ref> It was certified gold on April 4, 1968, the same day that [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] was assassinated, an event that may have helped the sales of the single.<ref name="riaa">{{cite web
 | url=  https://www.riaa.com/gold-platinum/?tab_active=default-award&se=bobby+goldsboro
 | title=Gold & Platinum - RIAA
 | work= [[RIAA]]
}}</ref> It was the best-selling record worldwide for 1968, even more popular than "[[Hey Jude]]".<ref name="Billboard74"/>{{rp|BG8}} It was a crossover hit, topping both the pop and country singles charts, one of only three songs to do so in the 1960s. 

The recording was nominated for two Grammy Awards in 1968: Record of the Year and Best Contemporary-Pop Vocal Performance, Male.<ref name="grammy">{{cite web
 | url=  https://www.grammy.com/artists/bobby-goldsboro/2394
 | title= GRAMMY Award Results for Bobby Goldsboro
 | work= [[The Recording Academy]]
 | date= 19 November 2019
 }}</ref> It was awarded Song of the Year in 1968 by the Country Music Association.<ref name="cma">{{cite web
 | url=   https://www.tennessean.com/picture-gallery/entertainment/music/2014/02/07/cma-awards-show-1968/5300065/
 | title= CMA Awards Show 1968
 | work= [[The Tennessean]]
 | date=  February 7, 2014
}}</ref>

Despite its popularity, the song was often dismissed or disparaged from the beginning. It has been called "innocuous pop",<ref name=perone>{{cite book
 | url  =https://books.google.com/books?id=gzl1lBFXKhQC&pg=RA2-PT127
 | title=The Album: A Guide to Pop Music's Most Provocative, Influential, and Important Creations [4 volumes]: A Guide to Pop Music's Most Provocative, Influential, and Important Creations
 | series=The Praeger Singer-Songwriter Collection
 | first=James E. | last= Perone
 | publisher=ABC-CLIO
 | year= 2012
 | isbn= 9780313379079
 | quote=The charts were still sprinkled with such innocuous pop as Bobby Goldsboro's "Honey" ...
}}</ref> "classy schlock",<ref name=christgau>{{cite web
 | url=  https://www.robertchristgau.com/xg/bk-aow/column5.php
 | title=Secular Music
 | first=Robert | last= Christgau
 | work= [[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]
 | date= November 1968
 | quote=[Joe] Tex's record closes with Bobby Goldsboro's "Honey," the classiest schlock of the year and the epitome of what is called modern country.
}}</ref> more "dreadful" than [[Luciano Pavarotti|Pavarotti]],<ref name=rodricks>{{cite web
 | url=  https://www.baltimoresun.com/1991/05/08/more-melodies-to-shoosh-kids/
 | title=More melodies to shoosh kids
 | work= [[The Baltimore Sun]]
 | first=Dan | last= Rodricks
 | date= May 8, 1991
}}</ref> and, hyperbolically, the "Worst Song of All Time" on 21 April 2006 by [[music critic]] Todd Leopold of [[CNN]] whose ambivalent antipathy left him "transfixed" by "one of the biggest songs of the year."<ref name=cnnleop>{{cite news |last1=Leopold |first1=Todd |title=The worst song of all time |url=http://www.cnn.com/2006/SHOWBIZ/04/19/eye.ent.worstsong/index.html?eref=sitesearch |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190206053156/http://www.cnn.com/2006/SHOWBIZ/04/19/eye.ent.worstsong/index.html |archive-date=February 6, 2019 |access-date=August 18, 2019 |website=Cnn.com |date=April 21, 2006
 | quote=I sat transfixed in my car as it played, as if I were in the midst of an accident. The simpering melody, the tearjerking lyrics: God, how I hated it. And yet I couldn't change the station.
}}</ref>
sections.text:
"Honey" was immediately and immensely popular. It sold a million copies in its first three weeks,{{rp|BG4}} the fastest-selling record in the history of United Artists. It was certified gold on April 4, 1968, the same day that Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated, an event that may have helped the sales of the single. It was the best-selling record worldwide for 1968, even more popular than "Hey Jude".{{rp|BG8}} It was a crossover hit, topping both the pop and country singles charts, one of only three songs to do so in the 1960s. 

The recording was nominated for two Grammy Awards in 1968: Record of the Year and Best Contemporary-Pop Vocal Performance, Male. It was awarded Song of the Year in 1968 by the Country Music Association.

Despite its popularity, the song was often dismissed or disparaged from the beginning. It has been called "innocuous pop", "classy schlock", more "dreadful" than Pavarotti, and, hyperbolically, the "Worst Song of All Time" on 21 April 2006 by music critic Todd Leopold of CNN whose ambivalent antipathy left him "transfixed" by "one of the biggest songs of the year."

[[Margaret Lewis (singer-songwriter)|Margaret Lewis]] released an [[Answer song|answer version]] titled "Honey (I Miss You Too)", which reached No. 74 on the country chart in 1968.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xwoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA36 |title=Billboard Hot Country Singles |date=July 6, 1968 |magazine=Billboard |page=36 }}</ref> A jazz instrumental version was recorded by [[Don Sebesky|The Distant Galaxy]] as a medley with the "[[Piano Concerto No. 21 (Mozart)|Elvira Madigan theme]]", and it reached No. 39 on the AC chart the same year.<ref name="hyatt"/> In 1969, [[O. C. Smith]]'s version of the song reached No. 44 on the pop chart, while [[Orion (singer)|Orion]] recorded a version that reached No. 89 on the country chart in 1979.<ref name="hyatt"/>
sections.text:
In 1968, Oscar Santana, an Ibersound recording artist had success with his version, making it to no. 1 on Latin American Single Hit Parade charts.

Margaret Lewis released an answer version titled "Honey (I Miss You Too)", which reached No. 74 on the country chart in 1968. A jazz instrumental version was recorded by The Distant Galaxy as a medley with the "Elvira Madigan theme", and it reached No. 39 on the AC chart the same year. In 1969, O. C. Smith's version of the song reached No. 44 on the pop chart, while Orion recorded a version that reached No. 89 on the country chart in 1979.
